## REASONING

The user's request is a two-year contrast of water partitioning — wet (1993) vs dry (2002) — in the Salt River headwaters. This is fundamentally a **forcing-period** experiment, and that is exactly a lever the framework can pull: run the same column set under two forcing windows and compare ET / surface runoff / sub-surface drainage / soil-moisture storage. That part is fully feasible.

The subtlety is the second candidate driver, **elevation** (900–3300 m — a large span crossing the rain-snow transition). Elevation matters here mostly through its control on temperature, precipitation phase, and snow. But the framework lacks elevation-downscaled forcing: a column set placed across elevation bands under a single uniform forcing would show *soil* variation, not an elevation/climate/snow signal. So I will NOT claim to isolate the elevation-on-partitioning mechanism. I stratify across elevation only to span domain heterogeneity of soils/land-surface, and I flag elevation-driven climate/snow as not-answerable with the missing capability recorded.

Two goals: (1) mechanistic — how partitioning shifts between a wet and dry year; (2) validation — against the only in-domain observation, USGS stream gauges. But a single-column ELM produces local runoff/drainage, not routed streamflow at a gauge; comparison requires runoff aggregation/routing, which is a capability gap. SNOTEL (the natural validator for the snow story) is sparse/missing, so snow validation is a gap, not a co-located check.

Sampling: the treatment is the year (2 levels), applied to a small stratified spatial set. I use 3 elevation bands × 2 dominant soil classes = 6 exploratory columns, each run under both years, concentrated in the snowmelt-influenced upper basin and valley/riparian zones where partitioning is most sensitive.
